title: What a Wallet Is
body:
A wallet in Web3 is not a place where money sits, but a tool that holds keys and credentials and uses them to prove things. The wallet holds a private key, which must never be shared, and a public address, which can be shared, and it signs statements on the owner's behalf. Understanding that the wallet holds keys, not coins themselves, is the first correction most newcomers need, because it explains why losing the key means losing access.

Most confusion about wallets comes from the name, which suggests a container, while the reality is a keyring.

The working method is wallet basics for everyday users. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Learn the two parts: a private key that is never shared, and a public address that can be shared
  2. Understand that the wallet proves things by signing, not by showing the key
  3. Back up the recovery phrase in a safe offline place, never in a photo or message
  4. Practice with a tiny, unimportant amount before any real use
  5. Never enter a recovery phrase on a website that asks for it

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Private key never shared; OK :: Public address understood as shareable; OK :: Recovery phrase backed up offline; OK :: Practice with unimportant amount first; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record offers education only, not financial advice, and it does not recommend any particular wallet. Wallet types, risks, and recovery options differ, and a later record compares custodial and self-held wallets directly. A common mistake is treating the wallet as a bank account with a reset button, when no such button exists for self-held keys. title: Public and Private Keys in Plain Language
body:
Public and private keys are a pair that works like a padlock and its key, except the padlock is public and the key is private. Anyone can use the public key to lock a message or verify a signature, while only the private key can unlock it or create a signature. The security of the whole system rests on one rule: the private key never leaves its owner's control, and anyone who learns it can impersonate the owner completely.

The pair is easy to picture and hard to overstate: the private half is the identity itself.

The working method is public-and-private key explanation. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Picture the public key as a padlock anyone may use
  2. Picture the private key as the only key that fits it
  3. Understand that signatures prove the private key was used, without showing it
  4. Keep the private key on the owner's device and in backup, nowhere else
  5. Treat anyone asking for a private key as a threat, without exception

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: MATCH :: Public key shared openly (public vs public); MATCH :: Private key kept secret (secret vs secret); MATCH :: Signature proves key use (proved vs proved); MATCH :: Recovery phrase stored offline (offline vs offline); matching: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all values match. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This explanation simplifies real cryptography, which involves algorithms and key formats this record does not detail. It teaches the mental model, not the mathematics, and it does not cover key generation security, which needs dedicated guidance for high-value use. A common mistake is sharing a private key with a support agent, a website, or a helpful stranger, for any reason. title: What a Blockchain Record Means
body:
A blockchain record means an entry in a shared ledger that many participants hold copies of, so changing one copy does not change the record. New entries are added in groups, linked to earlier groups, and agreed by the network's rules, which makes the ledger's history hard to rewrite quietly. The important consequence for everyday users is permanence: a record written to a public ledger is public and difficult to remove, which is a strength for proof and a weakness for privacy.

A shared ledger's power is that no single holder can quietly rewrite history, and its cost is that history is hard to erase.

The working method is blockchain record basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Picture many copies of one ledger, held by many participants
  2. Understand that new entries link to earlier entries
  3. Understand that agreement rules decide which entries count
  4. Treat public ledger entries as public and hard to remove
  5. Ask, before writing anything, whether it should be permanent and public

The output reads: OK :: Shared ledger picture understood; OK :: Linking of entries understood; OK :: Public and hard-to-remove understood; OK :: Permanence checked before writing; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. It does not cover investment, trading, or the environmental and economic debates around particular networks, which need their own sources. A common mistake is writing personal details to a public ledger and expecting later deletion to remove them. title: Decentralized Identity: You Hold Your Credentials
body:
Decentralized identity means credentials are held by the person they describe, rather than only by the company that issued them. A university, employer, or government office can issue a credential to a person's wallet, and the person then shows it where needed, without asking the issuer each time and without the issuer learning where it was shown. The shift is from asking permission to presenting proof, and it is the central idea of the whole pair.

Today's identity is mostly accounts held by others; decentralized identity moves the proof into the person's own hands.

The working method is decentralized identity basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Understand issuance: an issuer gives a credential to your wallet
  2. Understand holding: the credential lives with you, not only with the issuer
  3. Understand presentation: you show it where needed, without asking the issuer
  4. Understand minimization: show only the claim needed, not the whole credential
  5. Understand revocation: an issuer can withdraw a credential that is no longer valid

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Issuance understood; OK :: Holding understood; OK :: Presentation understood; OK :: Minimization understood; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Decentralized identity systems are still maturing, and availability, standards, and legal acceptance vary widely by place and use. This record teaches the model, not a promise that any particular credential will be accepted anywhere. A common mistake is assuming decentralized means unregulated or anonymous, when issuers, verifiers, and revocation still matter. title: Verifiable Credentials Explained
body:
A verifiable credential is a digital claim, such as a degree, a license, or an age check, that a verifier can check without contacting the issuer and without trusting the holder's word alone. The credential carries the issuer's signature, which the verifier checks against the issuer's public key, and it can be presented selectively, showing for example that the holder is over a threshold without revealing a birth date. Selectivity is the privacy advantage: proof without oversharing.

A credential that can be checked without a phone call, and shown without oversharing, is what makes decentralized identity practical.

The working method is verifiable credential basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Learn the three roles: issuer, holder, verifier
  2. Understand that the issuer's signature is what the verifier checks
  3. Understand selective presentation: show the claim, not the whole record
  4. Understand that a credential can expire or be revoked
  5. Practice with a low-stakes credential before any important one

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Three roles understood; OK :: Signature checking understood; OK :: Selective presentation understood; OK :: Expiry and revocation understood; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Verifiable credential standards and acceptance are still developing, and this record does not promise that any particular credential format will be accepted by any particular verifier. It teaches the model and the selective-presentation habit. A common mistake is showing a full credential when only one claim was asked for, which surrenders the privacy advantage. title: Recovery: Losing Access Without a Reset Button
body:
Recovery for self-held wallets and credentials has no reset button, because no company holds the key to reset. The recovery methods are planned in advance: a recovery phrase stored safely offline, trusted guardians who can help restore access, or a social recovery arrangement agreed before loss. The time to set up recovery is before it is needed, since after loss, the options narrow to whatever was arranged in advance, which is often nothing.

Self-held access is freedom with a price, and the price is paid in advance planning, not in fees.

The working method is wallet and credential recovery basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Set up recovery before any important use, not after
  2. Store the recovery phrase offline, never in photos or messages
  3. Consider trusted guardians or social recovery where offered
  4. Test recovery on an unimportant wallet first
  5. Review recovery arrangements whenever guardians or devices change

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Recovery set up before important use; OK :: Phrase stored offline; OK :: Guardians or social recovery considered; OK :: Recovery tested on unimportant wallet; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Recovery methods differ between wallets and systems, and some offer no recovery at all, which users must understand before entrusting anything important. This record does not recommend any particular recovery method for high-value holdings, which need dedicated advice. A common mistake is assuming a support team can reset a self-held wallet, and discovering too late that none exists. title: Choosing a Wallet Type: Custodial or Self-Held
body:
Choosing a wallet type means choosing who holds the keys: a custodial wallet means a company holds them and can reset access, while a self-held wallet means the user holds them and no reset exists. Custodial wallets are easier and recoverable, but depend on the company's honesty and security. Self-held wallets are independent, but their loss is final. The choice is a trade between convenience with dependence and independence with responsibility, and different uses reasonably choose differently.

There is no universally best wallet, only a wallet whose trade fits the use.

The working method is custodial versus self-held wallet choice. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Define what the wallet will be used for before choosing
  2. Compare custodial ease and recoverability against dependence
  3. Compare self-held independence against finality of loss
  4. Start with small, unimportant use while learning either type
  5. Review the choice as the use grows more important

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Use defined before choosing; OK :: Custodial trade understood; OK :: Self-held trade understood; OK :: Small-scale learning first; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record offers education only, not financial advice, and it does not recommend any particular wallet or company. Wallet offerings, terms, and risks change, and users should read current terms for any service they consider. A common mistake is choosing by popularity alone, without asking who holds the keys. title: Signing a Message: What Approval Means
body:
Signing a message in Web3 means using a private key to approve a specific statement or action, and the signature proves the key holder approved it. The critical habit is reading what is being signed: the exact action, the exact amount or permission, and the exact recipient, because a signature on a vague or misleading request can approve far more than intended. Never sign a request that cannot be read, and never sign under time pressure from a stranger.

A signature is an approval, and approvals given blindly are the most common Web3 loss.

The working method is message signing explained. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Read the exact action, amount or permission, and recipient before signing
  2. Refuse to sign requests that cannot be read clearly
  3. Refuse to sign under time pressure from a stranger
  4. Check the signing request against what you actually intend
  5. Keep a note of significant signatures and their dates

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Action, amount, recipient read; OK :: Unreadable requests refused; OK :: Time-pressure signing refused; OK :: Significant signatures noted; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Signing interfaces differ, and some requests are genuinely complex, which is why the habit is to refuse what cannot be understood rather than to guess. This record does not cover the technical format of any particular signature scheme. A common mistake is signing to dismiss a popup, which is how broad permissions are granted unknowingly. title: Tokens and Collectibles Basics
body:
Tokens and collectibles in Web3 are entries on a ledger that represent something: a unit of value, a membership, a ticket, or a unique item such as a digital collectible. Owning the token means controlling the key that the ledger associates with it, and the token's meaning depends entirely on what its issuer and community recognize it as. A collectible's image, for example, is often stored elsewhere, while the token itself is only the ownership entry, a distinction that surprises many newcomers.

A token is an entry plus a shared understanding of what the entry means, and the entry alone is not the thing itself.

The working method is token and collectible basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Understand that owning means controlling the associated key
  2. Understand that a token's meaning depends on issuer and community recognition
  3. Distinguish the token entry from any image or file it points to
  4. Check what happens to the token if the issuer or platform disappears
  5. Treat every token claim as unverified until its issuer and terms are checked

title: Smart Contracts in Plain Language
body:
A smart contract in plain language is a program stored on a ledger that runs its terms automatically when its conditions are met, without a human intermediary. The program's code is its terms, and once deployed, it usually cannot be changed or stopped easily, which is both its strength and its danger: it performs reliably, but a mistake in its code performs reliably too. Everyday users should understand that interacting with a contract means accepting its code as written, not its marketing description.

Code that runs itself is a promise that cannot be renegotiated, which is why reading its terms matters more, not less.

The working method is smart contract basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Understand that a contract is code that runs automatically
  2. Understand that deployed code is usually hard to change or stop
  3. Distinguish the code's actual terms from its marketing description
  4. Check who can change the contract and under what rules
  5. Interact only with contracts whose terms and risks are understood

title: Spotting Web3 Scams
body:
Spotting Web3 scams means recognizing the lures that are specific to wallets and tokens: fake support agents asking for recovery phrases, imitation websites and apps, giveaways that require sending funds first, and signing requests that grant broad permissions. The universal rule covers them all: no legitimate support agent ever asks for a recovery phrase or private key, no giveaway requires sending funds first, and no urgent message should override the signing habit of reading first.

Web3 scams work because they borrow the language of help, generosity, and urgency, and the defense is a rule that needs no judgment.

The working method is web3 scam recognition for everyday users. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Never share a recovery phrase or private key with anyone, for any reason
  2. Verify websites and apps through channels you already trust, not through links sent to you
  3. Refuse giveaways that require sending funds first
  4. Read every signing request fully before approving
  5. Report suspected scams through the platform and to a trusted adult or authority where loss occurred

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Recovery phrase never shared; OK :: Sites verified through trusted channels; OK :: Send-first giveaways refused; OK :: Signing requests read fully; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record teaches recognition, not recovery of lost funds, which is often impossible and needs prompt reporting to the platform and authorities. It does not cover investment fraud law, which varies by jurisdiction. A common mistake is believing a scam is obvious and therefore cannot catch you, since the convincing ones are designed for confident people. title: Revocation: Taking a Credential Back
body:
Revocation means taking a credential back, so that it no longer counts as proof even though the holder still possesses a copy. Issuers maintain revocation lists or statuses that verifiers check, and a credential's validity therefore depends on both its signature and its current status. Holders should understand that possession is not validity, that revoked credentials must not be presented as current, and that revocation is how stolen or mistaken credentials are withdrawn in a system without central accounts.

A credential's power lives in its status, not in its possession, and status can change after issuance.

The working method is credential revocation basics. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Understand that possession alone does not prove current validity
  2. Understand that verifiers check revocation status, not only signatures
  3. Learn how the issuer of each credential handles revocation
  4. Stop presenting a credential known to be revoked
  5. Ask verifiers what status sources they check before relying on a credential

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Possession distinguished from validity; OK :: Status checking understood; OK :: Issuer revocation method learned; OK :: Revoked credentials not presented; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Revocation systems differ in speed, privacy, and completeness, and a verifier that skips the status check undermines the whole system. This record teaches the model, not any particular revocation registry, and it does not cover legal disputes about wrongful revocation. A common mistake is presenting a revoked credential as current because the file is still in the wallet. title: Privacy on a Public Ledger
body:
Privacy on a public ledger is limited by design, because ledger entries are visible to anyone who looks, and patterns across entries can identify people even when names are absent. Addresses are pseudonyms, not anonymity: a single link between an address and a person, such as a purchase, a post, or a service account, can connect the whole history to that person. The defenses are restraint in what is written, separation of addresses for different purposes, and the assumption that anything on a public ledger is public forever.

Pseudonymity is a mask that slips once, and after it slips, the whole history wears a name.

The working method is privacy limits of public ledgers. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Treat every public ledger entry as public forever
  2. Understand that addresses are pseudonyms, not anonymity
  3. Separate addresses for different purposes where possible
  4. Avoid writing personal details to public ledgers
  5. Assume patterns across entries can identify a person

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Public-forever assumption adopted; OK :: Pseudonymity distinguished from anonymity; OK :: Addresses separated by purpose; OK :: Personal details kept off ledgers; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Use and limits. Privacy techniques for ledgers exist and are developing, but none makes a public ledger private by default, and this record does not recommend any particular technique. It teaches restraint and separation as the everyday defenses. A common mistake is believing an address without a name is anonymous, while its history tells a recognizable story. title: Identity Across Services
body:
Identity across services is the promise of decentralized identity in practice: one credential, shown to many verifiers, without creating a new account and password at each one. The benefit is fewer passwords and less repeated personal data, while the risk is correlation: verifiers that compare notes can link presentations, so selective presentation and separate credentials for separate purposes matter. The skill is choosing when one credential serves well and when separation protects better.

One credential everywhere is convenient, and convenience that links everything is also a profile.

The working method is one credential across many services. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Use one credential where the same claim is genuinely needed in many places
  2. Use separate credentials for separate purposes where correlation is a concern
  3. Present only the claim asked for, never the whole credential
  4. Track where each credential has been presented
  5. Revoke and replace credentials whose use has become too broad

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Shared claims identified; OK :: Separate credentials for separate purposes; OK :: Selective presentation practiced; OK :: Presentations tracked; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Cross-service identity acceptance is still uneven, and this record does not promise that any credential will be accepted by any particular service. It teaches the trade between convenience and correlation, which users must weigh for each use. A common mistake is using one credential for everything because it is convenient, and thereby linking every presentation. title: Web3 for Everyday Tasks
body:
Web3 for everyday tasks is a judgment skill: when does a shared ledger, a self-held credential, or a program-run agreement actually help, and when is an ordinary account simpler and safer. Web3 helps where proof must survive without trusting one company, where credentials must be shown without repeated disclosure, and where terms must run without an intermediary. Ordinary accounts help where recovery matters, where mistakes must be reversible, and where privacy requires data to be erasable, which public ledgers resist.

The right question is never whether Web3 is good, but whether it fits this task better than the ordinary alternative.

The working method is when web3 helps and when it does not. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List what the task needs: proof, recovery, reversibility, privacy
  2. Test whether a shared ledger genuinely improves the proof
  3. Test whether self-held credentials reduce disclosure or increase it
  4. Test whether automatic terms help or remove needed flexibility
  5. Choose the ordinary alternative when it fits better, without apology

It does not cover financial decisions, and its examples are illustrative, not assessments of any live service. title: Future Identity: Recovery, Guardians, and Inheritance
body:
Future identity covers the questions today's wallets and credentials raise for tomorrow: who recovers access when the holder cannot, who inherits credentials and digital assets, and how guardians act without becoming owners. The emerging answers are guardian arrangements, inheritance instructions kept with a will, and credentials designed to expire or transfer under stated conditions. Families should discuss these questions while the holder can still decide, because after incapacity or death, the holder's intentions are much harder to establish.

Identity outlives its holder's ability to manage it, so its future must be arranged while management is still possible.

The working method is future identity recovery and inheritance. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Discuss recovery guardians while the holder can still choose them
  2. Write inheritance instructions for wallets and credentials alongside a will
  3. Decide which credentials should expire, transfer, or be destroyed
  4. Tell executors where instructions live, without sharing keys in the instructions
  5. Review the arrangement whenever guardians, devices, or holdings change
